title: Objects All the Way Down
body: PowerShell isn't just another command shell — every single thing a cmdlet returns is a real .NET object with its own properties and methods, not a wall of plain text you have to parse yourself. That one design choice is why cyber operators lean on it constantly: you can filter, sort, and pipe real data between commands with total precision, whether you're enumerating processes on a box or automating a security sweep across hundreds of machines.
keyPoints: PowerShell cmdlets follow a strict Verb-Noun pattern with a singular noun: Get-Process, never Get-Processes.
Windows 10 ships with PowerShell 5.1 by default; typing pwsh drops you into PowerShell 7.x side by side, and exit returns you to the previous session.

title: The Pipeline: Passing Objects, Not Text
body: Classic shells pipe raw text between commands, which means the receiving command has to re-parse that text to make sense of it. PowerShell's pipeline (|) passes whole objects instead — so a filter like Where-Object can reach directly into a real property on a real object, no string-parsing required. A typical pipeline reads left to right: get some objects, filter them down, keep only the properties you care about, then decide how to display the result.
keyPoints: Objects in PowerShell are passed through pipes based on their inputted cmdlets — the whole object travels, not just its printed text.
Format-Table and Format-List only change how the final result is displayed; they don't change the underlying objects.

title: Every Cmdlet Returns an Object — Prove It With Get-Member
body: Run Get-Process | Get-Member and PowerShell tells you exactly what you're holding: the object's TypeName (System.Diagnostics.Process) plus every property and method available on it. Properties are what you know about the object — Name, Id, Handles. Methods are what you can do to it — Kill(), Start(). That's why (Get-Process notepad).Kill() and Stop-Process -Name notepad both stop the same process: one calls the .NET method directly, the other is the cmdlet wrapper around it.
keyPoints: Get-Process | Get-Member | Where-Object {$_.Membertype -match "Method"} isolates just the methods, filtering out the properties.
Different object types expose completely different members — Get-EventLog -LogName System | Get-Member looks nothing like Get-Process | Get-Member.

title: Filtering With $_ and Where-Object
body: $_ is the pipelined variable — inside a Where-Object script block, it always means "the object currently passing through, from whatever came before it in the pipeline." Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Stopped"} reads naturally once you see it: for each service object flowing through, keep it only if its Status property equals "Stopped." There's also a shorthand form — Get-Service | where Status -eq "Stopped" — that skips the script block and $_ entirely but returns the exact same result.
keyPoints: $_ is always the same object type as whatever the previous pipeline stage produced.
The shorthand form is -Property -Operator Value, e.g. where Handles -GE 1000, with no curly braces or $_ needed.

title: Execution Policy: Restricted by Default
body: Because a .ps1 script can contain anything — including malicious code — PowerShell ships locked down. The default Execution Policy is Restricted, which blocks every script that wasn't created in the local intranet zone or a workgroup. Get-ExecutionPolicy -List shows the policy for every scope at once (Machine, User, Process...), and Set-ExecutionPolicy changes it for a given scope. This is exactly the kind of control a cyber operator needs to understand both to defend a box and to know what a compromised one might have quietly changed.

rows.label: Restricted
cells: Default. No scripts run at all — only individual interactive commands.

rows.label: AllSigned
cells: Scripts run only if signed by a trusted publisher.

rows.label: RemoteSigned
cells: Local scripts run freely; anything downloaded must be signed.

rows.label: Unrestricted
cells: All scripts run, with a warning shown for downloaded ones.

rows.label: Bypass
cells: Everything runs — nothing is blocked or warned about.

keyPoints: Restricted is the out-of-the-box default on a fresh Windows install.
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy Unrestricted -Scope CurrentUser changes the policy for just the current user, not the whole machine.

title: PowerShell Remoting: WinRM Replaces DCOM
body: PowerShell Remoting (since v2) lets you run commands on another machine entirely, using WinRM (Windows Remote Management) instead of the older DCOM. That's a deliberate security upgrade: WinRM needs only one firewall port open, defaults to Kerberos authentication, and encrypts every session with a per-session AES-256 key. Outside an Active Directory domain — or when connecting by raw IP address, which breaks Kerberos — you fall back to NTLM, and the target has to be explicitly added to the client's TrustedHosts list first.
keyPoints: WinRM defaults to port 5985 for HTTP and 5986 for HTTPS (which needs a certificate configured).
Setting TrustedHosts to "*" trusts every host on the network — fine for a quick lab test, a real security risk anywhere else.

title: Profiles: Making Aliases and Functions Stick
body: Create an alias or a function interactively and it vanishes the moment you close the window — by design, nothing persists automatically. A PowerShell profile is a plain .ps1 script, not created by default, that PowerShell checks for and runs automatically every time a matching session starts. There are four possible profiles, checked in order from lowest to highest precedence, so a setting in your own Current User, Current Host profile always wins over a machine-wide one.

steps.label: Current User, Current Host — highest precedence, yours alone

keyPoints: New-Item -ItemType File -Path $PROFILE -Force creates the Current User, Current Host profile if it doesn't exist yet.
$PROFILE | Get-Member -Type NoteProperty reveals the paths to all four possible profile files, even the ones that don't exist on disk.

title: Ready to Drill
body: You now have the core mental model: PowerShell moves real objects through a pipeline, every object exposes properties and methods you can inspect with Get-Member, Where-Object filters that pipeline with either a script block or shorthand syntax, Execution Policy locks scripts down by default, and Remoting/profiles extend all of it across sessions and machines. Head into the practice terminal and try the commands yourself before you drill — muscle memory sticks better than reading alone.
keyPoints: Verb-Noun cmdlets, singular nouns, dash-prefixed (or positional) parameters.
The pipeline passes whole objects, not text — Get-Member always tells you what you're holding.
$_ means "the current pipeline object"; Where-Object also has a shorthand -Property -Operator Value form.
Default Execution Policy is Restricted; WinRM (not DCOM) powers Remoting; profiles make customizations persistent.

title: Data Hiding in Plain Sight
body: Windows NTFS lets a single file carry more than one stream of data, but only the main stream shows up in a normal directory listing. Adversaries exploit this to stash scripts, payloads, and stolen data inside files that look completely ordinary in size and content. As a cyber operator, you need to know the exact commands that reveal these hidden streams, because tools like dir, type, and even a quick file hash check will not tell you they exist. This module walks through how Alternate Data Streams work, how to find them, and why they can undermine your trust in a simple hash comparison.
keyPoints: ADS can hide entire scripts or executables inside an ordinary-looking file
Standard tools like dir and type do not reveal ADS content
Editing an ADS does not change the file's hash

title: What Is an Alternate Data Stream?
body: Alternate Data Streams were introduced to NTFS back in Windows NT 3.1 as Microsoft's attempt at filesystem forks, built to keep NTFS compatible with other filesystems such as Apple's HFS+ and Novell's NWFS and NSS. Every NTFS file is made up of attributes, security settings, a mainstream, and any alternate streams attached to it. By default, only the mainstream is visible to a user browsing files or running a normal directory listing. Legitimate Windows features rely on ADS too, storing metadata like file attributes, icons, and image thumbnails, but the same mechanism can just as easily hide something an operator never intended to be there.

layers.label: Mainstream
layers.sub: visible by default - the $DATA everyone sees

keyPoints: Introduced in NT 3.1 for cross-filesystem compatibility
Only the mainstream is visible by default
Legit uses include icons, thumbnails, and file attribute metadata

title: Five Things Every Operator Should Know About ADS
body: Alternate Data Streams have a specific set of behaviors that matter operationally. They can be scanned by antivirus - Windows Defender Smartscreen, for example, is ADS aware - so ADS is not automatically invisible to security tooling. Writing to or altering an ADS does not change the file's MD5 hash, which is significant for anyone relying on hashing for integrity checks. An ADS is stripped away if the file is ever copied to a FAT32 volume, since FAT32 does not support streams, and NTFS provides no setting to disable ADS support entirely.
keyPoints: AV can be ADS-aware (Smartscreen is one example)
ADS content does not affect the file's MD5 hash
Copying to FAT32 strips the ADS; ADS cannot be disabled on NTFS

title: Finding ADS from an Elevated Command Prompt
body: In Command Prompt, echo content > file.txt:streamname writes an Alternate Data Stream onto file.txt, but a plain dir or type on that file shows absolutely no change - the ADS stays invisible to both. To confirm a stream exists, dir /R lists its name and size, shown as file.txt:streamname:$DATA, though this only proves the stream is there without showing what is inside it. To actually read the content, you need more < file.txt:streamname or open it directly with notepad file.txt:streamname; trying type file.txt:streamname instead throws a syntax error, since type cannot process a stream path.
keyPoints: dir and type never show ADS by default
dir /R proves a stream exists without revealing its content
more < file:stream or notepad file:stream reads the content; type on a stream errors out

title: Directories Can Carry ADS Too
body: Alternate Data Streams are not limited to files - directories can carry them as well. The lesson demonstrates this by creating a directory named kids and writing top-secret information into an ADS called kids:hidden.txt. Running dir /R kids shows the stream attached to the directory itself, listed as .:hidden.txt:$DATA alongside the directory's own $DATA entry, and more < kids:hidden.txt reveals the hidden content. This matters operationally because an investigator who only checks files for hidden streams could walk right past a payload stashed on a folder.
keyPoints: ADS can attach to a directory, not just a file
dir /R on a directory reveals its streams the same way it does for files
Never assume only files need to be checked for hidden streams

title: Finding ADS from PowerShell
body: PowerShell has its own set of cmdlets for working with streams. Set-Content -Path file.txt -Value "..." -Stream secret.info writes an Alternate Data Stream, while Get-ChildItem and a plain Get-Content on the file both show no visible change, just like their CMD counterparts. To actually surface every stream on a file, Get-Item file.txt -Stream * lists them all, including the mainstream, labeled with a Stream property of :$DATA, alongside any alternate streams labeled with their own names. Once you know a stream's name, Get-Content file.txt -Stream secret.info reads its content directly, and piping the Get-Item output through select FileName,Stream trims the result down to just the two properties that matter.
keyPoints: Get-ChildItem and plain Get-Content are blind to ADS
Get-Item -Stream * enumerates every stream on a file
The mainstream shows as :$DATA; alternate streams show their given name

title: Weaponizing an Alternate Data Stream
body: The same mechanism used to store a thumbnail can just as easily store an attack. In the lesson's demonstration, Write-Output creates an innocent-looking test.txt, and a series of Add-Content -Path test.txt -Value '...' -Stream secret.vbs calls write VBS script code into a hidden stream rather than into the file itself. Get-Content on test.txt still shows only 'Nothing to see here!' - the malicious code is completely absent from the normal view. Running wscript .\test.txt:secret.vbs invokes the Windows Script Host directly against the stream, executing the hidden VBS code, which in the demo simply opens a shell and pings 8.8.8.8, but could just as easily establish persistence or grant access for an attacker.
keyPoints: Add-Content -Stream can smuggle executable script code into an ADS
wscript can execute VBS code directly out of a stream path
Get-Content on the file alone will never show the hidden payload

title: The Hash That Doesn't Move
body: After running the malicious VBS stream, the lesson checks certutil -hashfile test.txt MD5, edits the ADS content with notepad, and hashes the file again - the MD5 hash comes back identical both times. That is because hashing reflects the mainstream, the actual $DATA content, and changes made only to an alternate stream never touch it. This is the single most important operational takeaway in the module: an operator cannot assume a file has not been tampered with just because its hash is unchanged, since an entire malicious script can be added, edited, or removed from an ADS without moving the hash at all.
keyPoints: MD5/file hashes reflect only the mainstream ($DATA)
Editing, adding, or removing ADS content leaves the hash unchanged
An unchanged hash is not proof a file hasn't been tampered with

title: Recap: Streams You Can't See Are Streams You Must Check
body: Alternate Data Streams let NTFS attach hidden data - legitimate metadata or a malicious payload - to any file or directory, visible only through the right commands. You've seen how dir, type, Get-ChildItem, and plain Get-Content all miss ADS entirely, while dir /R, more <, notepad, Get-Item -Stream *, and Get-Content -Stream can find and read it. You've also seen the sharpest edge of this feature: an ADS can carry and execute malicious code while leaving the file's hash completely untouched. Run through the drill questions now to lock in the commands, the syntax, and the hash-integrity gotcha before you move on.
keyPoints: Know the blind commands vs. the revealing commands, in both CMD and PowerShell
ADS can hide and execute malicious code (e.g., via wscript)
An unchanged file hash never proves an ADS-free file

title: Why Linux Command-Line Skills Matter
body: After you gain access to a target system, there's often no desktop, no mouse, and no icons to click — just a prompt waiting for input. Every real cyber operation eventually comes down to typing the right command with the right arguments, fast, under pressure. Bash gives you speed, the ability to scale up multiple actions at once, and the power to automate repetitive work with scripts, which is exactly what separates a fluent operator from someone flailing at a terminal. This module builds the foundation: commands, automation, the file system, and the string-manipulation tools you'll use constantly to find the signal in the noise.
keyPoints: CLI advantages over GUI: speed, scaling, automation
Bash is often the only interface available after gaining access
Fluency here underlies every later Linux module

title: Commands, Arguments, and Situational Awareness
body: Bash does four things: it executes commands, redirects their output, parses text input and output, and accepts scripts to automate all of that. Commands like pwd run alone, but most take arguments that change their behavior, like ls versus ls -l for a long listing. When you don't know a command's options, --help gives a quick summary and man gives the full manual page. The moment you land on a new system, a handful of commands establish situational awareness: who you are, what host you're on, and what the network looks like around you.

nodes.label: sudo -l
nodes.sub: What can I run as root?

keyPoints: --help and man give built-in documentation
pwd, whoami, hostname/uname -a establish who and where you are
sudo -l reveals available privilege-escalation paths

title: Variables, Command Substitution, and Redirection Streams
body: A variable stores a string value and is set without a dollar sign but read with one, so a=100 then echo $a prints 100. Command substitution, written $(command), assigns a command's output to a variable instead of a literal string, so directories=$(ls /) captures a full directory listing. Every command's output travels through one of three numbered streams: standard input is 0, standard output is 1, and standard error is 2. The > operator redirects output to a file and overwrites it, a numbered redirect like 2> sends just the errors somewhere, and >> appends instead of overwriting.

rows.label: Standard Input
cells: Default source for a command's arguments

rows.label: Standard Output
cells: Default destination for successful command output

rows.label: Standard Error
cells: Default destination for failed commands or errors

keyPoints: $(command) captures a command's output into a variable
0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr
> and 2> overwrite a file; >> appends

title: Piping: Chaining Commands Together
body: Piping uses the | character to send one command's standard output directly into another command's standard input, letting you chain tools instead of running them one at a time and manually copying results. A classic example is ls -Rlisa /etc | grep syslog, which lists every file under /etc and then filters that huge listing down to just the lines mentioning syslog. Errors don't disappear just because you piped — a permission-denied message from ls still prints to the screen unless you also redirect standard error, for example with 2> /dev/null before the pipe. Piping is the single habit that turns a handful of simple commands into a powerful investigative workflow.
keyPoints: | sends stdout of one command into stdin of the next
2> /dev/null before a pipe silences errors
Piping chains simple tools into complex filters

title: Automating Work: For Loops, If Statements, While Loops
body: A for loop needs a collection of objects assigned to a variable, a loop variable representing the current item, and a command to run against each item — it naturally terminates when the collection runs out. If statements evaluate a comparison as true or false and branch accordingly, commonly written as a one-liner like for object in $objects; do if [ -d $object ]; then echo directory; else echo file; fi; done. A while loop keeps running as long as its condition stays true, re-checking that condition after every iteration, which means a poorly written while loop whose condition never turns false will run forever. Knowing the difference between a loop guaranteed to end (for) and one that isn't (while) is critical before you run automation against a live system.
keyPoints: For loops end automatically when the collection is exhausted
While loops re-check their condition every iteration and can run forever
if/else branches on true/false comparisons

title: The Linux File System Hierarchy (FSH)
body: Every Linux distribution, from Ubuntu to Debian, follows the same File System Hierarchy standard, so once you know it on one box, you know it everywhere. Root, written /, is the doorway everything else hangs off of. /bin holds essential commands like ls and echo that any user can run, /home holds a directory for every non-root user, /etc holds host-specific configuration for things like networking and firewall rules, and /var holds variable data, including the system's logs by default. Underneath a file system sits a partition, and underneath that sits the physical media itself — the FSH is just the top, human-facing layer of that stack.
keyPoints: /etc = configuration, /var = logs, /home = user directories
/bin holds commands every user can run
The FSH standard is consistent across Linux distributions

title: Users, Groups, and the rwx Permission Model
body: Every Linux user has a unique UID recorded in /etc/passwd alongside their username, an x marking where their encrypted password lives in /etc/shadow, their GID, a comment field, home directory, and default shell. Groups work the same way through GID values in /etc/group, and every user automatically belongs to their own personal group in addition to any supplementary groups listed there. File and directory access is controlled by three permission sets — User, Group, and Others — each capable of Read, Write, and Execute, written as letters like rwx (relative) or as numbers like 7 (octal, since read=4, write=2, execute=1). Permissions mean different things on files versus directories, and critically, a file's own permissions never override a lack of read or execute permission on its parent directory.

rows.label: Execute (x / 1)
cells: Run the file as an executable

keyPoints: UID/GID identify users/groups; stored in /etc/passwd and /etc/group
rwx = 4/2/1; combine for octal values like 7
Directory permissions govern access even if a file's own permissions allow it

title: Special Permissions and the String-Manipulation Toolkit
body: Two special permission bits change normal behavior: the sticky bit, common on shared directories like /var/tmp, stops anyone but a file's owner (or root) from deleting it even if they have write access to the directory; and SUID/SGID, shown as an s in the user or group field of ls -l, force an executable like /bin/ping to run with the permissions of its owning user or group instead of whoever launched it. Once you can navigate the file system, you need to make sense of its text output, which is where grep, awk, sed, and regular expressions come in. grep searches input for patterns, often written as regex, and prints matching lines; awk reformats or extracts specific fields from text using a delimiter, useful for building tables from command output; and sed is a stream editor that rewrites text on the fly, such as sed s/root/bacon/g to swap one string for another as it streams past.

rows.label: grep
cells: Searches text for patterns (regex) and prints matching lines

rows.label: awk
cells: Reformats/selects text fields based on a delimiter

rows.label: sed
cells: Stream editor — rewrites text as it passes to output

keyPoints: Sticky bit protects files from deletion by non-owners in shared directories
SUID/SGID run an executable as its owning user/group (shown as 's')
grep filters, awk reformats/extracts fields, sed rewrites text

title: Recap: You Now Speak Bash
body: You've covered the core toolkit: running commands with arguments and finding help, using variables and command substitution, controlling output with redirection and streams, chaining tools with pipes, and automating repetitive work with for, if, and while. You've also mapped the Linux file system from root down to /etc and /var, learned how UID/GID and rwx/octal permissions gate access to files and directories, met the sticky bit and SUID/SGID special permissions, and picked up grep, awk, and sed for slicing through text. That's the same toolkit real operators use every day to gain, hold, and understand access to a system. Head into the drill questions now while the commands and syntax are still fresh.
keyPoints: Commands + automation + file system + permissions + text tools = full toolkit
Drill now to lock in the syntax before it fades
This foundation underlies every later Linux-based module

title: Why Cyber Operators Study the Boot Process
body: The boot process is the automated sequence that takes a machine from a powered-off state all the way to a logged-in desktop. Antivirus and security tooling traditionally do not load until after the kernel and boot drivers have already started, which leaves a window where malware can gain a foothold with the same privileges as the operating system itself. Rootkits and bootkits are built specifically to exploit that window, hiding themselves and other malicious code before defenses ever wake up. A cyber operator who understands each stage of the boot process, and the tools like BCDEdit used to inspect it, can recognize when that chain has been tampered with and use the same knowledge during offensive operations.
keyPoints: Rootkits load before antivirus software does
Boot process = power button to logged-in desktop
Understanding each stage helps detect (or exploit) tampering

title: The Three Phases of Booting
body: Windows breaks the boot process into three broad phases: hardware initialization, loading the boot sector or boot manager, and loading the operating system from that boot sector. Only certain portions of this lengthy process can be interacted with easily, which is exactly why attackers who can influence any phase gain an outsized advantage. Each phase is also a potential target: firmware-level rootkits attack the earliest phase, while bootkits attack the boot manager phase specifically. The rest of this module walks through each phase in more depth, along with the tools operators use to inspect them.
keyPoints: 3 phases: hardware init, boot sector/manager, load OS
Only limited portions are user-interactable

title: Rootkits: Hiding Before the Antivirus Wakes Up
body: A rootkit is malware that hides itself and other applications, typically running in kernel mode so it shares the operating system's own privileges and can sometimes start before the OS does. Because anti-malware software traditionally does not load until after the kernel and boot drivers do, rootkits exploit weaknesses at different points in startup. An exposed operating system compromised this way can be used to further offensive goals such as pivoting to other systems or stealing data. Knowing the four categories below tells you exactly which stage of the boot process was subverted.

rows.label: Firmware Rootkit
cells: The PC's BIOS or other hardware firmware
Starts before the OS even loads

rows.label: Bootkit
cells: Loads the bootkit before the OS

rows.label: Kernel Rootkit
cells: A portion of the OS kernel

rows.label: Driver Rootkit
cells: A boot driver used to talk to the PC
Pretends to be a legitimate boot driver

keyPoints: Rootkits run in kernel mode with OS-level privileges
4 types: firmware, bootkit, kernel, driver

title: BIOS vs UEFI: Firmware, Boot Loaders, and How to Tell Them Apart
body: BIOS and UEFI are firmware, software coded onto non-volatile memory such as ROM, EPROM, EEPROM, or flash memory, and both verify critical hardware like SATA drives, display adapters, and SDRAM before handing off to the next stage. BIOS locates the MBR and runs the boot loader stored there: NTLDR on Windows 2003 and older, bootmgr on Windows 7 Service Pack 1 and newer. UEFI instead reads a GPT-based EFI system partition holding bootmgfw.efi, the Windows Boot Manager, and adds benefits like faster boot times, easier flash/EEPROM updates, a Secured Boot mode that only allows verified drivers to load, and support for drives up to 9 zettabytes versus BIOS's 2-terabyte limit. To tell which one a machine is running, filter bcdedit output for "winload" (winload.exe means BIOS, winload.efi means UEFI), or check the BIOS Mode field in Msinfo32.exe.
keyPoints: winload.exe = BIOS, winload.efi = UEFI
UEFI adds Secure Boot (verified drivers only)
Msinfo32.exe's 'BIOS Mode' field also reveals this

title: From Kernel to Logon: Five Steps
body: Once a boot loader hands off, Windows System Initialization runs through five steps: loading the operating system kernel, initializing the kernel, starting subsystems, starting Session 0, and starting Session 1. In step one, winload.exe (BIOS) or winload.efi (UEFI) reads the BCD to load essential disk drivers and then the kernel itself, ntoskrnl.exe; if the machine is resuming from hibernation, winresume.exe reads hiberfil.sys instead. In step two, ntoskrnl.exe loads the Windows Registry and device drivers, starts the pagefile at C:\pagefile.sys, and loads hal.dll, which abstracts hardware interfaces for the kernel. Once the kernel finishes loading it spawns the System process, which in turn spawns the session management processes smss.exe and csrss.exe.
keyPoints: ntoskrnl.exe = the Windows kernel
hal.dll abstracts hardware for the kernel
System process spawns smss.exe and csrss.exe

title: Starting Subsystems: Kernel Mode vs User Mode
body: smss.exe, the Session Manager Subsystem, loads environmental variables like %APPDATA% and %COMPUTERNAME%, populates the pagefile, starts the kernel and user mode subsystems, and starts a csrss.exe for each user subsystem it creates. The kernel subsystem creates and manages every resource Windows has by talking to drivers, controlling things like system power state, process and thread creation, graphical rendering, and Access Control Lists via the Security Reference Monitor; users cannot interact with it directly, though its activity is observable through logs and debugging tools. The user subsystem is the first part of Windows a user can actually manipulate: it manages user applications, process creation, internet connectivity, and object access through API calls to hal.dll, and it runs in both Session 0 and Session 1.
keyPoints: smss.exe = Session Manager Subsystem
Kernel subsystem is not directly user-interactive
User subsystem runs in Session 0 and Session 1

title: Session 0 vs Session 1: Services and the Desktop
body: Session 0 is reserved for security and high-privilege processes such as services, isolated from individual users. wininit.exe marks itself critical, initializes the Windows temp directory, loads the rest of the registry, and starts lsm.exe (Local Session Manager) and lsass.exe (Local Security Authority Subsystem, which authenticates users and generates access tokens); services.exe, the Service Control Manager, then loads AutoStart services using LSASS to authenticate them. Session 1 and up are standard user sessions: each spawns its own csrss.exe, then winlogon.exe (which by default prompts for credentials via logonui.exe), then userinit.exe (which creates an account token and a custom environment), and finally explorer.exe as the graphical desktop. Because Session 0 processes run as SYSTEM, they can be tricked into executing malicious commands via services, while Session 1's hundreds of auto-started processes are a common target for registry-key and script-based persistence.

rows.label: Session 0
cells: Security & high-privilege services, isolated from users
SYSTEM — higher than an admin account

rows.label: Session 1+
cells: Interactive desktop for each logged-on user

keyPoints: Session 0 = SYSTEM privilege, runs services
Session 1 = interactive logon via winlogon.exe -> userinit.exe -> explorer.exe
Both are common persistence targets (MITRE ATT&CK)

title: BCDEdit: Analyzing and Repairing Boot Configuration
body: When Windows boot settings become corrupted, bcdedit is the tool used to inspect and fix them; running bcdedit alone lists every Boot Manager and Boot Loader entry, each identified by a tag like {bootmgr} or {current}. Operators back up and restore the BCD with /export and /import, modify an entry's description or path with /set {identifier}, add a brand-new entry with /create, control which entry loads first with /displayorder, and remove one entirely with /delete {identifier} /f. bcdedit can also toggle troubleshooting options, such as /set {default} safeboot minimal to force Safe Mode, or /set {bootmgr} timeout 29 to change how long the boot menu waits. Only one Windows Boot Manager should ever exist on a system, but more than one Windows Boot Loader entry is expected and simply indicates a dual-boot system.
keyPoints: bcdedit lists/edits entries by {identifier}
Only one Boot Manager should exist; multiple Boot Loaders = dual boot

title: Recap: From Power Button to Desktop
body: You've now traced the full arc: hardware initialization finds a boot loader via BIOS's MBR or UEFI's EFI partition, that loader hands off to winload, which loads ntoskrnl.exe and hal.dll, and five system-initialization steps carry the machine from kernel to a fully interactive Session 1 desktop. Along the way, rootkits and bootkits exploit the gap before anti-malware software loads, Session 0 concentrates SYSTEM-level services that make an attractive attack surface, and BCDEdit gives operators a way to inspect, back up, and repair the whole chain when something breaks or was tampered with. Run through the drill questions now to lock in the sequence, the process names, and the commands you'll actually use in the field.
keyPoints: 3 boot phases -> 5 system-init steps -> Session 0/1
BCDEdit inspects and repairs boot configuration
Rootkits/bootkits target the gap before AV loads

title: Every Stage Is an Attack Surface
body: The Linux boot process takes a machine from powered-off to fully functional through a strict sequence of firmware, bootloaders, kernel, and init scripts. A skilled adversary can tamper with any single stage to plant persistence, hide from detection, or seize early control before security tools even start. As a cyber operator, knowing exactly what runs, where it lives on disk, and what file controls it is what lets you tell a locked-down system from one riddled with default vulnerabilities.
keyPoints: Boot is a sequence of stages, each running specific programs
Adversaries can alter any stage to further their goals
Understanding each stage's configuration options is core to defense and offense

title: The Boot Process at a Glance
body: The full journey runs firmware first, then two bootloader stages, then the kernel, then init, then post-boot shell setup. Each stage hands control to the next: firmware checks hardware and finds the boot sector, the first bootloader locates and hands off to GRUB, GRUB loads the kernel, the kernel spawns init, and init brings the system to a target level of functionality before the user shell environment loads. Memorizing this order is the backbone for everything else in this module.
keyPoints: Six stages, each handing off to the next
Firmware runs and exits before Linux even starts

title: BIOS vs. UEFI: Firmware That Starts It All
body: BIOS and UEFI are firmware, not software, stored in non-volatile memory (ROM, EPROM, EEPROM, or Flash) that does not clear itself on restart. Both do the same fundamental job: verify critical hardware like SATA drives, display adapters, and SDRAM, then locate the MBR or GPT. UEFI has mostly replaced BIOS because it boots faster, is easier to patch since it lives in flash/EEPROM, supports Secured Boot to only allow verified drivers, and handles drives up to 9 zettabytes versus BIOS's 2-terabyte ceiling.
keyPoints: Firmware lives in non-volatile memory
UEFI's Secured Boot only allows verified drivers to load

title: The MBR: 512 Bytes That Matter
body: The 1st stage bootloader is either the Master Boot Record (MBR) or GUID Partition Table (GPT) -- whichever the firmware locates. The MBR occupies exactly the first 512 bytes of a hard drive: 446 bytes of bootstrap code, four 16-byte partition entries, and a 2-byte boot signature (0x55 0xAA) that tells Linux it's looking at a valid MBR. Tools like lsblk show you the disk and partition layout, while xxd or dd let you inspect or copy those raw 512 bytes directly for forensics.

diagram.caption: MBR = 446B bootstrap + 4x16B partition entries + 2B signature (0x55 0xAA) = 512 bytes

keyPoints: MBR = 512 bytes total: bootstrap code + 4 partition entries + boot signature
GPT is the modern replacement: UEFI-only, redundant, up to 128+ partitions, up to 9 zettabytes

title: GRUB: The 2nd Stage Bootloader
body: GRUB's only job is to load the Linux kernel the user chooses. On legacy MBR/BIOS systems, GRUB Stage 1 (boot.img) lives in the first 440 bytes of the MBR and loads Stage 1.5 (core.img), which sits between the bootstrap and the first partition; Stage 2 (normal.mod) then loads the grub menu and reads /boot/grub/grub.cfg to list available kernels. On UEFI/GPT systems, Stage 1 is instead grubx64.efi on an EFI partition or in /boot, going straight to Stage 2. In grub.cfg, the 'linux' command is what actually loads the kernel file, such as /boot/vmlinuz-4.15.0-76-generic -- never edit this file casually, since a mistake can leave the system unable to boot.
keyPoints: GRUB's one purpose: load the chosen Linux kernel
grub.cfg's 'linux' command loads the actual kernel file

title: The Kernel: Monolithic and Modular
body: The kernel is the heart of the OS, controlling memory management, device management, I/O requests, and CPU process scheduling. Linux's kernel is monolithic: all that functionality is exposed to programs through system calls, the mechanism every program uses to request kernel services -- tools like ltrace -S can show you these calls happening live, such as open, read, and write on a file. At the same time it's modular: modules extend base functionality without requiring a kernel rebuild, and if one module fails, only its functionality stops -- the machine keeps running.
keyPoints: Monolithic: all functionality reachable through system calls
Modular: modules add functionality without a rebuild; a failed module doesn't crash the system

title: Init: SysV Run Levels vs. Systemd Targets
body: Once loaded, the kernel is hard coded to execute /sbin/init, which brings the system to a target level of functionality using an initialization daemon. Legacy SysV reads /etc/inittab for a default run level (0-6, e.g. 1=single-user no network, 5=multi-user with networking and GUI) and runs Kill/Start scripts named Knn/Snn in /etc/rc#.d, symlinked to /etc/init.d -- the number sets execution order. Modern systemd instead links /sbin/init to /lib/systemd/systemd and reaches a default.target (usually graphical.target) built from Wants= (soft dependency, failure doesn't stop the target) and Requires= (hard dependency, failure stops the target) statements in unit files.
keyPoints: Kernel hard-codes execution of /sbin/init
SysV: run levels + Knn/Snn scripts. Systemd: targets + Wants/Requires units
If the default run level fails, SysV falls back to run level 0 (halt)

title: Inspecting Systemd With systemctl
body: Because systemd wires together hundreds of interdependent unit files across eleven possible directories, hunting through the filesystem by hand is impractical -- systemctl is the tool built for the job. 'systemctl list-dependencies graphical.target' shows the dependency tree, 'systemctl show -p Wants graphical.target' lists everything a target wants to start, 'systemctl list-unit-files' enumerates every unit systemd sees, and 'systemctl cat graphical.target' prints a unit file's actual contents. Finally, init spawns a login on each virtual console via getty, which invokes /bin/login to prompt for and verify credentials -- the last step before a user gets a shell.
keyPoints: systemctl is the practical way to query systemd's web of dependencies
getty + /bin/login is the last step of init, producing the login prompt

title: Post Boot: The Adversary's Favorite Playground
body: After init, a chain of shell configuration files shapes every user's environment -- and because they're just plain text and scripts, they're easy for an attacker to quietly modify. /etc/environment sets global variables (like PATH) for everyone, read once at Init completion; it's part of PAM, not a bash script, so it needs a restart to take effect. /etc/profile runs system-wide for every interactive login, sourcing /etc/bash.bashrc and any *.sh in /etc/profile.d. Per-user, .bash_profile (a.k.a. .profile) runs only on an interactive LOGIN shell (e.g. fresh ssh session), while .bashrc runs only on an interactive NON-LOGIN shell (e.g. spawning a nested bash). Because adversaries can plant a command in any of these to run automatically at login, checking them is a standard part of evaluating a Linux system.

layers.label: /etc/environment
layers.sub: global vars, read once at Init

keyPoints: These files are the easiest boot-stage files for an adversary to abuse
Know which file fires on login vs. non-login, global vs. per-user

title: From Firmware to Shell Prompt
body: You've now traced the full path: BIOS/UEFI firmware finds the MBR or GPT, a 1st stage bootloader hands off to GRUB, GRUB loads the kernel, the kernel spawns init (SysV run levels or systemd targets), and post-boot scripts finish shaping the user's shell. Every stage has its own files, tools, and quirks -- and every stage is a place a skilled adversary might hide or a defender might look. Run the drill questions now while the sequence, file locations, and command names are fresh.
keyPoints: Six stages: firmware, 1st stage bootloader, GRUB, kernel, init, post boot
Each stage has specific files and tools worth memorizing for real system evaluation
Drill now to lock in the sequence and details

title: The Cyber Operator's X-Ray Vision
body: A Windows box can have hundreds of processes running at any moment, and malware wants to blend into that crowd rather than stand out. Attackers rename their tools to look like svchost or drop them next to legitimate services precisely because operators glance past what looks normal. Process Validity is the skill of telling known-good from possible-bad by attributes and behavior, not by blind trust. On offense it protects your own toolset from exposure; on defense it's how you catch an intruder before sensitive data — or a mission — is lost.
keyPoints: Malware hides by mimicking or hooking legitimate processes, files, registry keys, and drivers
Matters for both OCO (protect your toolset) and DCO (defend the network)
The lesson calls this literally life-and-death for soldiers on mission

title: Processes, DLLs, and Services: Know Your Building Blocks
body: A process is simply a running program, whether a user double-clicked it, like Chrome or Notepad, or it's working quietly in the background, like a spell checker. A DLL is different: it's a non-standalone chunk of code that can't run by itself, so it has to be linked into a host process like RUNDLL.EXE to execute, which is exactly why malware loves hiding inside one. A Service is a long-running executable that lives in its own Windows session, can auto-start at boot or logon, can be paused and restarted, and never shows a user interface. The lesson treats processes, services, and daemons as the same underlying concept.

rows.label: Runs on its own?
cells: No — needs a host exe like RUNDLL.EXE

keyPoints: DLLs cannot be directly executed — they need a host exe like RUNDLL.EXE
Services run silently, with no UI, and can auto-start at boot or logon

title: Three Ways to Look: PowerShell, CMD, and GUI
body: Every category you'll investigate — processes, services, scheduled tasks, network connections — can be viewed three ways on a Windows host: a PowerShell cmdlet, a classic Command Prompt tool, and a GUI application. Knowing both the PowerShell and CMD command for each category matters because you won't always have PowerShell available, and the two outputs expose different details. This pattern repeats throughout the module, so memorizing the pairs now pays off on every later command you run.
keyPoints: Get-Process/tasklist, Get-Service/sc query, Get-ScheduledTask/schtasks, Get-NetTCPConnection/netstat
GUI options include Task Manager, services.msc, Task Scheduler, and TCPView

title: Digging Deeper: PPIDs, Modules, and Service Details
body: Plain Get-Process won't show you a process's parent — for that you need Get-CimInstance Win32_Process, which exposes ParentProcessId so you can see what launched what. To see which DLLs a process has loaded, pipe Get-Process through foreach {$_.modules}, or use tasklist /m for the same view at the command line; tasklist /svc instead shows which services live inside each process, since one svchost.exe host can run several services at once. On the services side, get-service ALG | format-list * unpacks a service's full configuration, including its StartType, while sc queryex type=service exposes each service's PID; to see the exact path a service launches from, use Get-Ciminstance Win32_service | Select Name, ProcessId, Pathname.
keyPoints: Get-CimInstance Win32_Process exposes ParentProcessId; Get-Process does not
tasklist /svc shows which services run inside each host process

title: Scheduled Tasks: A Favorite Persistence Trick
body: Scheduled Tasks launch a program or script when a condition is met — a preset time, machine boot, or user logon — which makes them a convenient way for an attacker to establish persistence and have malware fire off automatically. In the lesson's demo, a task named IchBinBosh was configured to run every 15 minutes, and its Task To Run field showed powershell.exe running a Base64-encoded command, a classic way to hide what a task really does from a casual glance. Get-ScheduledTask in PowerShell lists tasks, but its Settings and Triggers are obscured; schtasks /query /tn "IchBinBosh" /v /fo list in Command Prompt reveals far more, including that encoded command. CyberChef is the tool the lesson points to for decoding a string like that.

nodes.label: Script/malware called
nodes.sub: separate file does the real work

keyPoints: Get-ScheduledTask hides Settings/Triggers detail; schtasks /query /v /fo list reveals it
Encoded PowerShell in a task is a red flag — decode it with CyberChef

title: Autorun Registry Keys: Whose Autoruns Are These?
body: Beyond the Task Scheduler, Windows has several registry Run keys that launch programs automatically, and the scope of each key matters. HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run affects every user on the local machine, HKCU\...\Run affects only the currently logged-on user, and HKU\<sid>\...\Run lets you target a specific user by their SID even when they aren't logged in. Each of those keys also has a RunOnce sibling, and HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services plus the ServiceGroupOrder/GroupOrderList keys control which services load and in what order — all worth checking when hunting persistence.
keyPoints: HKLM = all users, HKCU = current user, HKU\<sid> = one named user
Every Run key has a RunOnce counterpart

title: Spotting the Fakes: Abnormality Checklist
body: Once you know what normal looks like, abnormal starts to jump out. Watch for misspelled process names, like scvhost instead of svchost, and a process running from the wrong directory — legitimate system binaries live in C:\Windows\System32, not C:\Program Files or a temp folder. Also watch for non-standard ports, like HTTP traffic on port 808 or 880 instead of 80, and duplicate instances of a process that should be unique, such as two smss.exe, especially if one carries an unusually high PID. The lesson's 'Where's Waldo' task list exercise ties it together: a high-PID duplicate smss.exe, an unfamiliar bad.exe, and a misspelled reqedit.exe were the three giveaways.

steps.label: Duplicate 'unique' processes with a high PID

keyPoints: System processes run from C:\Windows\System32; third-party ones run elsewhere
bad.exe, reqedit.exe, and a high-PID duplicate smss.exe were the Where's Waldo tells

title: Recap: Trust, But Verify Every Process
body: You now have the full toolkit: what a process, DLL, and service actually are; the PowerShell/CMD/GUI command pairs for processes, services, scheduled tasks, and network connections; where scheduled tasks and registry Run keys hide persistence; and the checklist of red flags — misspellings, wrong directories, odd ports, duplicate PIDs — that separate known-good from possible-bad. This is exactly the judgment call you'll be asked to make in the CTFd challenges and on real missions, so drill the commands until Get-Process, tasklist /svc, schtasks /query /v, and netstat -anob feel automatic.
keyPoints: Run the drill questions now to lock in the commands and red flags
Process Validity is a judgment skill — practice it until it's automatic
